sources.citation: Dutton, T.E. 1975. South-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum Languages. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol 1, pp. 613-666. Pacific Linguistics C-38. DOI 10.15144/PL-C38.613
sources.note: Only a family-wide generalisation for all South-East TNG languages, p. 622: 'Some languages are tonal but stress is generally important and related to intonation which may be quite complex.' Binahari section 2.9.5.5.4 (pp. 638-639) is geographic/dialectal only; 'None of the languages except Magi (or Mailu) has been studied or recorded in any detail.'

sources.citation: Thomson, N.P. 1975a. Magi phonology and grammar - fifty years afterwards. In T.E. Dutton (ed.), Studies in Languages of Central and South-East Papua, pp. 599-666. Pacific Linguistics C-29.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Section 2.5 Stress, p. 605: 'The stress on a word is usually on the second last syllable. Although it does sometime occur on the third last syllable, it never occurs on the last syllable in a polysyllabic word' - but this is MAGI/Mailu (mail1250), a sister language, not Binahari.

sources.citation: Thomson, N.P. 1975b. The dialects of Magi. In T.E. Dutton (ed.), Studies in Languages of Central and South-East Papua, pp. 37-90. Pacific Linguistics C-29.
sources.note: Section 2.12.3 Binahari (pp. 47-48): Ma and Neme'a share only 60% basic vocabulary and are treated as two separate Mailuan languages under the blanket name Binahari; comparative wordlists only, no stress.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2018. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics 4), 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. (Section 2.3.1.25 Mailuan.)
sources.note: Nothing on Binahari prosody. The Mailuan section gives location, that the Binahari pair and Bauwaki-O'oku pair are closely related while other Mailuan languages share c. 50% basic vocabulary (Dutton 1999), documentation status per language (Binahari and Binahari-Ma: 'wordlist: Ray 1938'; only Mailu has grammar sketches), Ross's Proto-Mailuan pronouns and pTNG reflexes in Mailu and Bauwaki. It is an authoritative 2018 confirmation that no description beyond wordlists exists for Binahari.

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University. xii+449 pp. (author entries Bastard 1919/1920, Strong 1919; language-index entries Binahari, Ma, Neme, Neme'a, Nemea.)
sources.note: Bibliography only; it establishes that up to 1996 the entire literature on Binahari/Neme'a consisted of two colonial vocabularies (Strong 1919, Bastard 1920), the Voegelin & Voegelin 1965 and Wurm & Hattori 1981 classification listings, and Thomson's 1975 Magi papers. No phonological description is indexed.

sources.citation: Summer Institute of Linguistics. 1985. Language Survey of Binahari [unpublished survey wordlist], as digitised in Greenhill, Simon J. 2015. TransNewGuinea.org: an online database of New Guinea languages (PLoS ONE 10: e0141563), source 'sil-1985', language 'binahari' (bina1275), 102 lexical items (lexibank/transnewguineaorg CLDF).
sources.note: Wordlist-only data: 102 forms in phonetic transcription with glottal stop, aspiration and offglides marked (e.g. maʔa 'mouth', ɛmɛkʰ 'man', debaʔaʰ 'moon', oᵘka 'neck') but no stress or pitch marks and no accompanying statement; not a statement source.

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom. 1982. Borrowing in Austronesian and non-Austronesian languages of coastal south-east mainland Papua New Guinea. In Halim, Carrington & Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, Vol 1, pp. 109-177. Pacific Linguistics C-74.
sources.note: Appendix 2 'Mailuan phonemes and the reconstruction of Proto-Mailuan' (pp. 162-165) gives tentative segmental inventories for Ma and Neme'a (5 vowels, open syllables, no clusters except Neme'a kw-); nothing on stress or accent.
